hints: Look closely at the word monoclonal and remember which part of an antibody actually touches the antigen, the variable tip or the constant stem?
For a phagocyte to engulf a virus, the antibody must act as a bridge with one end on the virus and the other end on the phagocyte. What happens to that bridge when the two ends are cut apart?
walkthrough:
**Recall antibody structure simply**

Think of an antibody like a Y shape. The tips of the Y are the variable regions, and they are the only parts that fit the antigen like a lock and key.

The stem of the Y is the constant region. It never binds antigen, it binds to phagocyte receptors.

**Apply monoclonal means identical**

Because this is a monoclonal antibody, every single molecule is identical and specific for one virus.

That means every variable region has exactly the same shape and will fit exactly the same epitope, or part, of the virus antigen. So statement 3 is correct and statement 1 is wrong.

**Check why phagocytosis now fails**

Normal opsonisation needs an intact antibody to link the two cells together: variable end on virus + constant end on phagocyte.

Here the ends are separated. The variable piece can still bind virus but cannot signal a phagocyte, and the constant piece can signal a phagocyte but cannot bind virus. No bridge means no engulfing, so statement 2 is wrong.

options.A: Both 1 and 2 are false. Constant regions do not bind antigen, and separated fragments cannot bridge virus to phagocyte.
options.B: Statement 1 is false because constant regions never bind antigen, even though statement 3 is true.
options.C: Statement 2 is false because phagocytosis by opsonisation needs an intact antibody to link virus to phagocyte.
options.D: Only statement 3 is correct. All variable regions from one monoclonal antibody bind the same epitope on the virus antigen.
